title: Delirium, not pepper spray, cited in man's death: Altercation with police: [Toronto Edition]
article: A Toronto man on a four-day cocaine binge who died en route to hospital after he was pepper-sprayed by police was likely suffering excited delirium, a rare medical condition triggered by his cocaine use that left him impervious to pain and on the verge of death, says Ontario's deputy chief coroner.

Dr. Jim Cairns, who worked on a landmark 1998 paper highlighting the condition, said witness accounts of a confrontation between Toronto police and Robert Walker early yesterday indicate the 41- year-old man had all the symptoms of excited delirium.

The condition, which can also affect those with severe psychiatric illness or alcohol withdrawal, is characterized by bizarre behaviour, hallucinations, an incredible burst of strength and an elevated body temperature.
"\[People with excited delirium\] have lost that control and are firing on all cylinders," Dr. Cairns said.
Ontario's Special Investigations Unit is investigating to determine what role, if any, Toronto police played in Mr. Walker's death.
Neighbours said police were called to Mr. Walker's east end residence after the man reportedly went berserk. He was punching walls until his hands were left a bloody pulp.

The confrontation moved to a cordoned-off Woodbine Avenue, north of Queen Street East, where Mr. Walker -- naked in subzero temperatures -- was surrounded by police who tried to subdue him with pepper spray, Priya Glassey, a witness, said.
"He was crazed. It was bizarre," said Ms. Glassey, who watched from her second-floor bedroom window. "From the way he was lunging at the cops, it looked like he had a knife."

Ms. Glassey said the standoff lasted about 10 minutes, during which officers sprayed Mr. Walker at least once with pepper spray. The spray inflames the mucous membranes and throat, making it difficult to breathe and leaving the recipient with a burning sensation.
"I saw them spray him once and it didn't do anything," she said.
Another resident, who declined to be named, defended officers' actions. "There was just commotion. 'Stay down,' \[police\] said," she recalled.
The woman, who also watched from her bedroom window, said: "They didn't touch him until after the pepper spray."
Mr. Walker was eventually brought under control and transported in a waiting ambulance to Toronto's St. Michael's Hospital.
"Paramedics were transporting Mr. Walker to hospital when he went into medical distress," a brief statement by the SIU said. The man was pronounced dead at the hospital.
In the mid-1990s, Ontario's Office of the Chief Coroner sent a memo across the country alerting colleagues to the condition.

"It said that people in this condition are in danger of dying at any time," he recalled. "If confronted, they will normally need to be restrained for their safety and the safety of other people. Once restrained, don't keep them lying on the ground. Get them up and immediately ship them to hospital."

Death is usually caused by an elevated blood pressure, increased heart rate or cardiac arrhythmia. Certain methods of restraining a suspect can act as a catalyst by restricting breathing and blood flow.
Dr. Cairns said Mr. Walker was properly restrained.

Rose Hong, a spokeswoman for the SIU, which probes all injury or death to civilians following a run-in with police, would not reveal the results of an autopsy conducted yesterday and likely won't until the conclusion of the investigation.
Dr. Cairns, who attended the autopsy but would not discuss the results, said a mandatory inquest will be called into Mr. Walker's death.
